definition: Turgid means swollen and overblown in style or language.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word turgid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know turgid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wine club's newsletter grew turgid under its new editor: a simple pinot tasting now 'unfolds across the palate's cathedral in vaulted arpeggios.'
Flowery prose stops short of turgid — the blossoms are decoration, but light still gets through and the sentence still moves.
Impenetrable goes further than flowery by every measure: where turgid writing is swollen and slow, impenetrable writing has sealed itself shut, and no reader gets in at all.

Overblown means puffed up bigger than the content deserves — a modest finding presented as a revolution. Turgid lives in the wording itself: swollen, pompous diction, sentence by sentence. A claim is overblown when its importance is exaggerated; prose is turgid when its dress is.

Bloated means swollen with sheer excess — too many pages, sections, and repetitions; the word suits budgets and bureaucracies as easily as prose. Turgid is a fault of style, not size: pompous, inflated diction that can strut in a single short paragraph. Bloated needs cutting; turgid needs plainer words.

Inflated language is pumped up with air, pretending to more weight than it has — grand words over a thin idea. Turgid gathers that inflation into a whole manner: swollen, ornamental, heavy on its feet. One phrase can be inflated; it takes a full style to be turgid.

Latin turgere ('to swell') produced almost nothing else in everyday English — botanists speak of a cell's turgor, but outside the greenhouse the family ends here. Learn turgid on its own, and let humid and rigid remind you what the -id ending does.
